stage_state.summary_md:
## Retirement Announcement

BA initially proposed coordinating a simultaneous retirement with Air France in October 2003, but Air France declined—choosing May instead, citing that France would never sanction a dual retirement perceived as celebratory after the accident.

The announcement was planned for an April 9th Forum 150 meeting until Bannister noted it coincided with the 34th anniversary of Concorde's first flight. The date shifted to April 10th, 2003. Bannister, in full uniform, delivered the news with a rehearsed slide presentation. The reaction split sharply: roughly two-thirds of senior managers expressed sadness; the remainder felt relief. No one was ambivalent.

Bannister then served as company spokesman. Key messaging stressed this was a commercial decision driven by factors beyond BA's control, with assurances customers would receive equivalent service via upgraded Club Class and First on 747s.

At the press conference, when asked why Concorde was being retired, Bannister instinctively offered what became the universal party line: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons"—despite internally believing it had been quite the wrong decision at the wrong time for the wrong reasons.

Common questions included why BA spent money restoring Concorde only to retire it, and why not give aircraft to Richard Branson. On Branson, BA anticipated three scenarios: success would prompt him to claim BA couldn't run a tea shop; failure would blame BA's maintenance; refusal would be characterized as bullying. The official response—that government funding meant BA couldn't transfer ownership—was a "cop-out containing just enough truth." A senior Virgin pilot actually thanked Bannister, saying "You're not really going to give Concorde to us, are you, Mike?" and, upon hearing "not a chance in hell," replied "Thank God… because it would probably send us bust!"

On retaining one aircraft for air shows: Concorde required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate—far higher standards than the Vulcan's "Permit to Fly." The £60 million annual infrastructure cost would rise by another £40 million, remaining constant regardless of fleet size. Even halved to £50 million meant £1 million weekly for a single aircraft. Airbus, focused on the approaching A380 and successful A320 family, refused to maintain the Type Certificate. Their air-intake computer technology remained proprietary and secret due to military aircraft applications. Another organization theoretically could have taken the Type Certificate, but Airbus was under no compulsion to transfer it and had strong incentives to retain the technical drawings.

By summer, public discourse shifted from retirement motives toward celebrating Concorde's legacy. Edward de Bono observed that Concorde appealed to both brain hemispheres—the analytically superb and artistically graceful. For Bannister, the simpler explanation sufficed: most Britons had developed a sense of individual ownership. "That's my Concorde up there."
